query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace interstitial boron (0.1–0.3 at %) to the equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni high-entropy alloy (HEA) and then applying 80 % cold- (or cryo-) rolling followed by short (≤2 min) 800 °C annealing will simultaneously raise 25 °C yield strength and Young’s modulus while retaining or improving uniform elongation and K_IC. Specifically, the treated alloy will show ≥1.0 GPa yield strength, ≥35 % total elongation, a ≥10 % increase in Young’s modulus, and fracture toughness ≥150 MPa·√m—an improvement of at least 30 % in the strength–ductility product relative to the same processing of the boron-free alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast, homogenised equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 (at %) alloy ingot with grain size ≈ 100 µm, no intentional interstitial additions.
generation.intervention: Arc-melt with 0.1–0.3 at % B, homogenise 1200 °C/24 h, 80 % cold- or cryo-roll (-196 °C), then anneal 800 °C/120 s followed by water quench.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical testing in air; oxygen and nitrogen kept <10 ppm during melting to avoid nitrides/oxides; cooling rate >100 °C·s⁻¹ after anneal to suppress boride precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Supersaturated interstitial B locked in the fcc lattice + heavily refined (0.5–1 µm) recrystallised grains with high dislocation density.
generation.mechanism: 1) Local lattice distortion from oversized interstitial B raises elastic modulus and Peierls barrier, increasing strength and modulus. 2) B segregates to grain boundaries, lowering boundary energy and suppressing cavitation, improving ductility and toughness. 3) Fine grains and boron-dislocation interaction promote continuous strain hardening that delays necking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to identically processed B-free CrMnFeCoNi, the B-added alloy will show: • +300–400 MPa yield strength, • +10 % Young’s modulus, • equal or +5–10 % total elongation, • ≥150 MPa·√m fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: Cold-rolled + annealed CrMnFeCoNi typically exhibits ~650–700 MPa yield strength, ~30 % elongation, 200 GPa modulus, K_IC ≈120 MPa·√m.
generation.boundary: Effect diminishes if B >0.3 at % (boride precipitation) or anneal >5 min (B depletion of matrix); not expected in bcc-dominated or ordered HEAs where B has low solubility.
generation.uncertainty: No systematic data yet exist on sub-0.5 at % B in CrMnFeCoNi; magnitude of modulus and toughness increases is extrapolated and may be smaller.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two 20 mm-thick plates: (A) baseline CrMnFeCoNi, (B) same +0.2 at % B. Apply identical 80 % cryo-rolling and 800 °C/120 s anneal. Machine tensile (ASTM E8) and compact-tension (ASTM E399) specimens. Measure Young’s modulus by resonant ultrasound spectroscopy before testing.
measurements: Atom-probe measured B content in matrix (at %)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if, relative to baseline, sample B shows: (i) yield-strength increase <100 MPa or (ii) Young’s modulus increase <5 % or (iii) strength–ductility product (σ_y × ε_total) not ≥30 % higher.
